Organization: humans and agents

Agents change who does the work. People still set intent, own outcomes and decide where not to automate. This page shows how the organization changes, from the book.

What changes

Agents absorb tasks, not jobs

A job is a bundle of tasks. Take each job apart, decide what happens to each task, then rebuild the role. Book, Ch 24

Five shifts in the operating model
ShiftBeforeAfter
Who does the workPeople using screensAgents and people together
What gets releasedCode and configurationAlso instructions, skills, models, limits and policies
How cost behavesMostly fixed licensesVariable use on several meters
What failsPrograms and interfacesAlso reasoning, context, drift and cost loops
Who is accountableProcess owner for the processProcess owner for process and agent outcomes

Four classes for every task

  • Absorb. The agent does it; a person audits samples. Typically L3 to L4.
  • Augment. The agent prepares; a person decides. Typically L1 to L2.
  • Retain. A person does it; the agent may inform. Typically L0 to L1.
  • New. Work that did not exist before, such as reviewing the weekly override report.

One clerk’s week, before and after

The book takes one accounts payable clerk’s job apart, task by task. Book, Ch 24.7.9

Common errors

  • Saved hours are not saved people. A 30% saving spread over 85 people frees nobody until roles are rebuilt.
  • Review time is real work. At L2, 2,000 proposals a week at 90 seconds each is 50 hours.
  • Do not hollow out the role. If only hard cases remain, the job exhausts people and the entry path closes.

Book, Ch 24. Figures are illustrative.

Org structure

Agents are owned, not managed

Agents appear on the org chart only as assets of a role. They have no reporting lines, no headcount and no place in spans of control. Book, Ch 24

Each team page lists its people. Under the role that owns them, it lists that role’s agents and their levels. The agent registry, not the HR system, is the agents’ record.

New roles and where they sit

Role catalog
RolePurposeReports toSizing driver (illustrative)
Agent business ownerAccountable for one agent’s outcomes, limits and riskProcess ownerOne per agent, part-time
Agent supervisorRuns the daily hand-off queueFunction managerOne per 3,000 to 6,000 exceptions a month
Agent instruction designerWrites instructions, skills and test casesAutonomy Office or product teamOne per 8 to 12 agents in active change
AgentOps analystMonitors health, drift and costAgentOpsOne per 15 to 25 agents in production
Evaluation engineerTest sets, red team, regressionAutonomy OfficeOne per 15 to 20 agents in production
AI controls analystControls over agents; audit evidenceInternal controlOne per 20 to 30 financial agents
AI FinOps analystMeter data, forecasts, showbackFinOpsOne per 4 to 6 vendor meters
Platform agent specialistAgent features of one platform; never owns agentsPlatform teamOne per platform with live agents

The Autonomy Office is the book’s name for the company’s AI center of excellence. It owns standards and the registry. It does not own business outcomes. Book, Ch 25

The agent business owner matters most

  • Approves the agent’s specification, level, limits and escalation paths.
  • Signs promotions on evidence and reviews overrides at least monthly.
  • Owns the agent’s risk and can stop the agent.
  • Is a business person, not IT. A cross-platform agent gets one owner for the whole outcome.

A vendor survey cited in the book found that only 9.5% of companies name a person formally accountable for agent behavior. Read it as directional. Book, Ch 22 and Ch 24

Spans, layers and what managers do now

  • Managers. Routine supervision shrinks. Reviewing agent output, handling exceptions and coaching grow.
  • Spans. Size them by human decision load, not headcount. AP might widen from 1:10 to 1:14, but only after review load is measured at L2.
  • Reviewer capacity. It sets how many agents a team can supervise. A higher hand-off rate needs more people, not a wider span.
  • Layers. Remove a layer only if it just relayed information the trace store now shows. Keep every layer that holds a decision right or a control signature.

Team shapes: human-led, agent-operated pods

Pod types
PodPeopleAgentsOwns
Run podProcess lead (agent business owner), 3 to 8 exception analysts, a supervisorThe agents of one process sliceDaily outcome, hand-off queue, override review
Build podProduct owner, agent and context engineers, an evaluatorAgents in build and shadow modeSpecifications, skills, test sets, releases
Control podAI controls analyst, evaluator, AgentOps analystGuardian agentsSeeded tests, trace completeness, control evidence

Career paths

Four new career paths
PathComes fromProgression (illustrative)
Agent business ownerProcess leads, senior analystsOne agent, then an agent family, then process owner
AgentOps engineerIT operations, site reliability, integrationAnalyst, engineer, on-call lead, AgentOps lead
Context and knowledge engineerBusiness analysts, data stewards, experienced role holdersContributor, engineer, domain lead for a value stream
EvaluatorQuality assurance, internal audit, analysts with statisticsEvaluator, evaluation engineer, evaluation lead

Pay and the junior pipeline

  • Agents are not span. Owning ten agents is not managing ten people. Grade roles by decisions owned and risk carried.
  • Pay for outcomes owned. Owners carry objectives on the agent’s outcome and control record, not its usage.
  • Keep a dual ladder. Context engineers and evaluators can reach senior grades without managing people.
  • Protect the junior pipeline. Keep a fixed graduate intake, an apprenticeship on real exceptions and monthly rotation through manual cases.
  • Fill new roles from inside first. Process knowledge matters more than AI knowledge.

Book, Ch 24 and Ch 25. Sizing drivers and progressions are illustrative.

Storyboard

One AP team, redesigned over 30 months

Follow the accounts payable team at Meridian, the book’s fictional company. People move to new roles before the agent depends on them. Book, Ch 24 and Ch 25

  1. 1

    Today

    A team buried in exceptions

    85 people process 900,000 invoices a year. About 432 exceptions a day, at 20 minutes each, need about 20 people.

  2. 2

    Month 3 · Gate G0

    Owners first, promises in writing

    The Autonomy Office starts. Owners are named for the pilots. The job commitment is announced before pilots, and consultation begins.

  3. 3

    Task map

    The job is taken apart

    Clean matching is absorbed. Variances and supplier queries are augmented. Override review and root-cause work are new tasks.

  4. 4

    Month 13 · Gate G1

    Role cards and the first run pod

    Role cards are published. The first cohort is trained before go-live. The first run pod forms for Americas AP.

  5. 5

    Month 16 · Shadow

    The clerk judges the agent

    The agent runs on live cases but acts on none. The clerk settles disagreements. Shadow results stay out of performance reviews.

  6. 6

    Month 18 · L2

    Approve, with a reason code

    The clerk approves each proposal and codes every override. Review load is measured before any span is widened.

  7. 7

    Month 22 · L3 in one entity

    A new role before the agent acts

    The clerk becomes an AP exception analyst. The analyst approves up to USD 25,000 but cannot change agent limits or bank data.

  8. 8

    Months 26 to 33

    Pods, supervisors and the line in charge

    About 108 hand-offs a day need about three supervisors. Run, build and control pods form. The line takes over all pods.

Illustrative figures from Meridian, the book’s fictional company. About 44% of the clerk’s time is released and absorbed by not refilling posts, not by redundancies. Everything outside the green band stays at L2. Book, Ch 24

Your exception queue: people today and with agents

The book sizes the people an exception queue needs before and after the agent. Enter your own volume and minutes. Book, Ch 25.3.6

Delegation and decision-making

Agents change how much is decided, not who may decide it

Every step has a level. People set it, on evidence, through a named body. Raising it needs a meeting; lowering it needs one person. Book, Ch 01, Ch 24 and Ch 25

The autonomy levels

Autonomy levels L0 to L5
LevelWho decidesHuman role
L0 ManualHumanDoes the work
L1 AssistHumanUses the agent’s suggestions
L2 ApproveAgent proposesApproves every action
L3 Act within limitsAgentHandles exceptions above limits; samples
L4 Run and reportAgentAudits, tunes limits and policies
L5 FullAgentSets goals only. A boundary marker, not a target, for postings

Levels are allowed levels, not capability. Capability sets what is possible. Governance sets what is allowed. The lower one applies. Book, Ch 22 See the scale and the default ceiling.

Who sets the level

Decision rights for autonomy changes
ChangeEvidence (summary)Decided by
L1 to L2Evaluation report; registered; roles approved; shadow exit metProcess product owner
L2 to L3, non-financial step3 months incl. a quarter-end; at least 1,000 actions; SLOs met; adoption gateOwner and risk lead
L2 to L3, triggers a posting or paymentSame evidence over three closes; limits outside the model; controls tested; audit consultedAutonomy council
L3 to L4Two quarter-ends at L3; strong harness score; error below target; audit cycle passedAutonomy council, endorsed by the risk council
Any downgradeAn incident or SLO breachOwner or AgentOps, at once

A vendor’s default setting is never the decision. Book, Ch 25

Decision rights by role

  • Process owners set intent and the do-not-automate list.
  • Agent business owners set limits within policy and stop their agents.
  • The autonomy council changes levels.
  • Any on-call engineer stops an agent, without a meeting.
  • The pod lead may route any case to people without approval. Demand for human judgment never waits for a meeting.

Ownership follows the layers. The CFO owns the limits. The CIO owns the harness and the inventory. The COO owns the boundary with physical operations. The CHRO owns role redesign. The chief risk officer and internal audit own the evidence standard. Book, Ch 01

RACI: A accountable, R responsible, C consulted, I informed
ActivityAccountableResponsibleConsultedInformed

Identity and scopesAgent ownerCISO / IAMAutonomy Office, controlDPO
Segregation of duties reviewInternal controlCISO / IAMOwner, Autonomy OfficeDPO

Exactly one accountable person per row. For anything that changes a financial control, that person sits in the business or risk line, never in IT alone. Book, Ch 22

Make approval limits executable

A delegation policy written for people is not a control for an agent. The harness checks each limit before the action, outside the model. Book, Ch 24

Policy text for people and executable rules for agents
Policy for peopleRule for the agent (illustrative)
Clerks may clear price variances up to toleranceRelease if under USD 500 and under 2% of line value; else route to the analyst queue
Managers approve invoices above USD 25,000The agent may prepare, never release; a named human role approves
No payment to changed bank details without call-backThe agent cannot change or use bank data changed in the last 30 days
Escalate supplier disputes after 10 daysA timer on the case opens a service case at day 10

Test each rule at the boundary (USD 499, 500, 501) before shadow mode and after every change.

Escalation paths

  • Outside its limits, the agent escalates with an evidence pack to a named queue. Book, Ch 01
  • Each step’s target card names the escalation queue and its response time, for example one business day. Book, Ch 01
  • Unanswered approvals go to a supervisor after one business day in the book’s AP example. Book, Ch 05
  • The person who approves an agent’s actions may not change its limits, instructions or tools. Book, Ch 24

One-way and two-way doors

The book does not use the one-way and two-way door framing. It uses reversibility and materiality instead. Irreversible actions, such as payments and external messages, stay at L2. Book, Ch 01 and Ch 22

Levels, limits and bodies are illustrative. Each company sets its own with internal audit.

Decisions with incomplete information

When the evidence is thin, route to a person

Agents rarely have every fact. The book’s answer: calibrate, set the threshold by cost, cite or say what is missing, and escalate when unsure. Book, Ch 03, Ch 05 and Ch 07

Act only above the threshold

Act automatically only when expected gain beats expected loss. The threshold p* = L ÷ (G + L) rises with the amount at stake. Book, Ch 03 The worked table is on Design choices.

A raw score is not a probability until it is calibrated. Use calibrated scores to route, never to approve. Book, Ch 07

Uncertainty bands

Three confidence bands
BandCalibrated confidence (illustrative)Route
Green0.95 or more, and all rails passAct at the step’s permitted level
Amber0.80 to 0.95, or one soft check failsConfirm with the person, or send to a reviewer
RedBelow 0.80, or any hard check failsFall back; do not act

Forecasts carry ranges, not single numbers. A cash buffer is set against the 10th percentile, not the median. Book, Ch 04

Cite, or say what is missing

  • Every factual claim needs a source. The output has a “missing information” field. An agent that cannot cite says what it lacks rather than guess. Book, Ch 05 and Ch 09
  • A decision without the required evidence is “not done”, for example a variance not computed by a tool. Book, Ch 05
  • A summary step that drops a missing-evidence flag is a control defect. Book, Ch 05
  • If input data fails its quality gate, the step is capped at L2. Book, Ch 01

The fallback ladder

  1. Retry with a tighter constraint.
  2. Ask the person a clarifying question. Agents tend to guess rather than ask, so make asking the cheaper path.
  3. Use a safe default, such as a promised call-back by a set time.
  4. Hand off to a person with the full context.
  5. Stop safely: no commit, and an open case.

Book, Ch 07. A fallback that never fired in testing is a hypothesis.

How a person decides on partial evidence

The approval card puts the gaps in front of the approver. A weak card produces rubber-stamping. Book, Ch 05

Approval card fields with an illustrative AP example
FieldIllustrative AP example
Proposed actionRelease one invoice for EUR 12,480
WhyThe contract allows an index adjustment up to 5%; the variance is 4.1%
Confidence and drivers0.91: clause match, index source, two prior adjustments accepted
What is missingThe supplier has not confirmed the index month
OptionsApprove; short-pay to the order price; ask the supplier; reassign
ReversibilityReversible until the payment run
DeadlineBefore the payment run; the discount expires in two days

Reversible or irreversible

Materiality and reversibility set the default ceiling. Small, easily reversed actions may reach L4. Irreversible ones stay at L2 or below. Book, Ch 01

An action that commits the company to a third party loses one level for its first 90 days at a new level. Book, Ch 01

Prove it small before you scale

  • Shadow first. The agent runs on live cases and acts on none. Book, Ch 24
  • Pilots end in a decision. Criteria are signed before the build and never changed after. A stop on evidence is a result. Book, Ch 26
  • Enough cases. About 300 clean cases show, with 95% confidence, an error rate below 1%. Below 0.3% needs about 1,000. Book, Ch 26
  • Treat estimates as hypotheses. Each has a baseline, a guardrail metric, a control group and a kill rule. Book, Ch 21
  • Vendor numbers are claims to test. Ask: production or demo, same baseline, review cost included? Book, Ch 21

What the book does not cover

The book has no general method for executive judgment under uncertainty. It treats incomplete information at the level of each step, through thresholds, evidence gates and pilots. It mentions value of information only as a routing rule: use the cheapest engine that clears the threshold. Book, Ch 21

Internal vs external agents

Credibility and trust: whose agent is it, and what has it earned?

Your own agents are owned, registered and inside your controls. Outside agents act for someone else. Treat each one like a new trading partner that never sleeps. Book, Ch 23

Two kinds of agent

Internal agents compared with external agents
QuestionInternal agentExternal agentSource
Who is it?Yours: built or bought, with a named business owner and technical owner.A supplier’s, bank’s, customer’s or distributor’s agent calling your systems. You still name an owner on your side.Ch 05, Ch 10, Ch 23
Where is it recorded?The enterprise registry. No registry, no run.Its own registry record, with a trust tier.Ch 05, Ch 23, Ch 25
How is it identified?Its own identity on every platform. Delegated tokens name the agent as actor, for one target, for minutes.A signed, short-lived record on the partner’s verified domain, then your own short-lived credential.Ch 03, Ch 23
What may it do?What its agent contract and autonomy level allow, L0 to L5.Only the filtered tools you publish for it. Read before write.Ch 05, Ch 10, Ch 22
How is it stopped?Your kill switch, through your gateways.Revocation at your gateway, within five minutes (illustrative), tested from both sides.Ch 05, Ch 23

How agents differentiate

Six things separate a credible agent from a claim. Ask for each before you widen what an agent may do.

  • Identity. One identity per agent, never a shared technical user. Calls without an agent identity are blocked. Book, Ch 02, Ch 23
  • Provenance. A record signed by a key bound to the partner’s verified domain. A signed card proves who published it, not that the agent is safe. Book, Ch 03, Ch 23
  • Declared capability. A claim, never a permission. Scopes come from your onboarding, as for an EDI trading partner. Book, Ch 22, Ch 23
  • Track record. Trust tiers are earned over time. An outside agent reaches action only after 90 days of reads without a material finding (illustrative). Book, Ch 23
  • Verifiable outcomes. Traces carry one correlation ID from request to payment, so an auditor can follow every decision. Book, Ch 14, Ch 25
  • Cost and contribution. A monthly scorecard per agent: tokens, energy and cost per completed outcome, attributable value and net contribution. No account, no promotion. Book, Ch 25

Capability sets the ceiling of what is possible. Governance sets the level allowed. The lower one applies. Book, Ch 22

How trust is earned and verified

  1. Discover. Read the partner’s published card. It is a hint only and never grants a scope.
  2. Verify. Check signature, domain, contract and the partner’s master record.
  3. Credential. Issue your own short-lived credential. No shared keys.
  4. Sandbox. Run the agent on synthetic data for two to four weeks; security tests must pass.
  5. Scope. Publish a filtered list of typed, versioned tools. Read before write.
  6. Limit. Cap rate, value and data volume per partner and per tool, at the gateway.
  7. Monitor. Baseline behavior and alert on deviation.
  8. Promote or revoke. The owner and the CISO sign a promotion. Revocation takes effect within five minutes.

Book, Ch 23. Durations and limits are illustrative.

Trust tiers for outside agents
TierWhat the agent may doEntry evidence
T0 UnknownNothing. Requests are logged and refused.None
T1 SandboxCall test tools on synthetic data.Verified identity and a signed contract annex
T2 ReadRead its own records through filtered tools.Sandbox passed; owner and CISO sign
T3 Act within limitsCreate or update cases and requests within caps.90 days at T2 without a material finding

No tier allows payment release, bank-data changes, credit-limit changes or user administration. No outside agent may change payment instructions until identity, authority and liability are settled with the counterparty. Book, Ch 13, Ch 23

The controls behind trust

  • Authentication. Verify the partner’s signing key, domain and contract before the first call. Book, Ch 23
  • Scoped permissions. Least privilege: start with read, elevate only when a privileged action is first needed. Book, Ch 23
  • Signed actions. Every write carries a delegated token whose current actor is the agent. Never pass a token through. Book, Ch 05, Ch 23
  • Audit trails. One trace store and one correlation ID across platforms. Book, Ch 14, Ch 22
  • Reputation. The book’s version is the trust tier: time at a tier without findings, owner sign-off and a tested revocation. Book, Ch 23
  • Certification and attestation. The partner signs a capability record that must validate against your schema. You still map its skills to your scopes. Book, Ch 23
  • Limits that grow with evidence. Promotion needs evidence and a human gate; demotion is automatic. Book, Ch 01, Ch 23
  • Kill switch. Contain first, classify second. Pin and hash every external tool, skill and model version. Book, Ch 23

Four kinds of trouble at the front door

Four threats from outside agents and the first response
ThreatWhat it isFirst response
Rogue agentA real partner agent that drifts after a model update or bugThrottle to the tier below; tell the partner owner
ImpostorSomeone posing as a partner’s agentDeny at the gateway; revoke and rotate; call the partner out of band
Injection carrierA genuine agent whose messages carry hidden instructionsTreat the text as data; quarantine the message
Poisoned componentA bad tool, skill or model update every trusting agent loadsQuarantine the version; roll back; list every agent that loaded it

Book, Ch 23.

Agent-to-agent negotiation risks

  • Loops. Two agents can call each other without end. Set a hop limit in the contract, a cost cap and a circuit breaker. Book, Ch 02
  • The message overrides the contract. Take terms from the contract, never from the other agent’s message. Book, Ch 06
  • No improvising. A negotiating agent works inside an envelope a person approves: objective, walk-away, allowed and forbidden levers, at most three rounds. Book, Ch 14
  • No leaks, no promises. Never disclose another supplier’s price. Every message says “subject to approval”. Counsel reviews disclosure and competition law first. Book, Ch 14
  • One voice. One owner of outside communication per customer per day. Book, Ch 13
  • Write it down. Two agents that negotiate or hand off work with judgment need an agent contract. Book, Ch 29

What the book does not cover

The book is silent on cross-company reputation scores for agents, on third-party certification of agents, and on two companies’ agents negotiating end to end, including collusion and deadlock.

  • Practice: treat an outside reputation score like a card. It is a hint and never grants a scope.
  • Practice: ask for third-party attestation in the contract annex, and keep your own sandbox and tiers.
  • Practice: when both sides are agents, cap rounds on your side and send any deadlock to a named person.

Practice items are common approaches, not from the book. Meridian figures are illustrative.
